fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. Luke says "…everyone went to his own town to register." (Luke 2:3) No one big gathering place, just people heading to their own towns. I think a LOT of people were packing a bag at the same time.

Rome is a big name, so I get why you went there. But the text says "…everyone went to his own town to register." (Luke 2:3) Luke doesn't send them all to one faraway city. That would be one LONG line, friend.

The temple is a big, holy place, so it's a fair guess. But Luke doesn't send everyone there. He says "…everyone went to his own town to register." (Luke 2:3) The place is each person's own town, wherever that was.

Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), is a famous name, so I see the pull. But Luke says Joseph "…was from the house and line of David." (Luke 2:4) Bethlehem is called the city of David in the same verse. Aaron isn't in this story.

Saul was Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:24), so you're in the right neighborhood with a king. But Luke names a different one. Joseph "…was from the house and line of David." (Luke 2:4) David is the name on Bethlehem's sign.

That's the reason Luke gives. Mary laid Him in a manger "…because there was no room for them in the inn." (Luke 2:7) The text says nothing more about why, so I won't guess. I think anyone who has ever shown up somewhere with no room left knows that sinking feeling.
Elijah, the prophet, does show up later in Luke (Luke 9:30), but not here. In this scene "…an angel of the Lord stood before them…" (Luke 2:9) No prophet is mentioned in this field.
Close, but no. The angel says the good news "…will be for all the people…" (Luke 2:10) He's speaking to the shepherds, but the news isn't limited to them.
Right, baker. The angel says it is "…good news of great joy that will be for all the people…" (Luke 2:10) He's speaking to the shepherds, but the news reaches way past them. That's a big circle.
That's the one. The angel says, "He is Christ the Lord!" (Luke 2:11) He also says a Savior has been born in the city of David. That's the news the angel hands those shepherds on their night shift.
I see why a priest came to mind, friend. But the angel doesn't call this baby a priest. He says, "He is Christ the Lord!" (Luke 2:11) That's the title the angel gives.
Yes, baker. The text says "…they hurried off…" (Luke 2:16) No slow stroll for these shepherds. I think I'd have been running with my apron flapping.

Right on, friend. They "…spread the message they had received about Him." (Luke 2:17) These shepherds saw the Child and spread the word instead of keeping it quiet. I think it would've been hard to keep quiet after a night like that.

Doubt is a fair human reaction, but it's not the one Luke gives. He says "…all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them." (Luke 2:18) Hearing a message like that, I bet I'd have needed a minute to sit down.

That's it, friend. Luke says "…Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart." (Luke 2:19) All who heard the shepherds were amazed, but Mary treasured these things and thought them over in her heart. That's a quiet kind of keeping.

Telling people is what the shepherds do (Luke 2:17), not what Luke shows from Mary. He says "…Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart." (Luke 2:19) The text doesn't have her telling the town.
You got it, baker. Luke says "The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen…" (Luke 2:20) I bet they came back feeling like different people.
